utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, are you following the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. It's Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, assisted this morning by Skye Winner, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning to you. Appearances for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: David Cunningham and Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you. So let's proceed, Ms. Korner. Good morning to you, Mr. Jokic. Ms. Korner is going to proceed with her cross-examination. I just take the opportunity to remind you that you are testifying for all intents and purposes under oath, on the basis of the solemn declaration that you entered yesterday. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Ms. Korner: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that note, His Honour yesterday said you had a right to seek the Judges's approval not to answer any question. There are some matters this morning that I'm going to be touching on that if you feel you do not wish to answer the questions on the grounds it may incriminate you, you can seek the Judges' leave. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told the Court yesterday that you retired from the VRS in 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So even though you were in charge of the civilian control at the Banja Luka airport, nonetheless, you still remained part of the military?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to go back, then, to one question. Are you telling this Court that before you retired from the military, you destroyed your workbook?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even though it was possible that you could have been called upon to produce an account of your movements at any period up until 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't think that anyone would request that of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear us now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed, Ms. Korner, and sorry. My apologies for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. I quite understand. It's obviously important that all three of you can hear what's being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. Please proceed, Ms. Korner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can I just confirm: You were transferred from Mostar to Banja Luka in about end of October/beginning of November 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I wasn't actually transferred; I just received a different assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until then, had you just been an ordinary pilot, a lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This information is not correct. At that time I was already a major in Mostar. I was promoted into the rank of major in the month of July 1991, and while I was in Mostar, I was deputy commander of a squadron.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stayed in the Banja Luka -- the position you were in Banja Luka as a squadron commander until August of 1992, didn't you, when you were transferred -- or when you became the flight controller?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less until August. There was a transitional period of handover, when you're sent to a new duty, there has to be a handover between the previous commander and the new one. So a certain period of time is necessary for -- to become familiar with the new duties. So this was this transitional period. I did not become flight controller, but the chief of flight control service at the airfield.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I apologise, but in fact I put that to you from what you told the investigators in July of 2001, in the interview, which I know you've had a copy of, where you said, and this is the top of page 5, and I'm not going to ask you to look at it: "At some point in August 1992, I became a chief of the airport flight control, and I stayed at that position until the end of war." Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, but a moment ago you asked me whether I had become a flight controller, and I corrected you. I told you that I had become the chief of airport flight control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. It was my error, and I apologise for that. Now, finally, before we move on to some different matters: You told us yesterday that there were your own personal records and the records of the unit. Where were the records of the unit kept? Where were they archived?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the unit was operational, and while I was the squadron commander, there was a metal safe where documents were kept, documents relating to the unit, active documents, so to speak. All those documents, if a document had been completed or if a book had been completed, were handed over, not immediately, but when documentation was being organised, those documents would be handed over and placed into the safe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Once they were no longer current documents, where did they go? In other words, where are they now? That's what I'm asking you, Mr. Jokic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the organisation of the squadron and the flight unit, there is an administrator. I don't know exactly what the procedure was once the documents were handed over, but it is my assumption that the documents could be found somewhere at the command of the air force. But again, this is only my assumption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is the command of the air force today? In Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it is at the Zaluzani Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is just outside Banja Luka; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts. Six or seven kilometres from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's where the headquarters of the Republika Srpska air force is, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I said, that this is where the command of the air force is located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the other matter that we touched on yesterday was any reminders you were given about the application of the Geneva Conventions to this conflict. I'd like you to have a look, please, at P382.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid I don't think this is on my list because it was something that I came across last night, but we can put the English on the ELMO. Well, Your Honour -- it's all right. We can pull that down so we can --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is part of the Official Gazette of the Serbian People. Just read, would you, to yourself, the order on the application of the rules of international law of war, and let me know when you've read it.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I received here a decree on the implementation of the material obligation. This is not a copy of the document that we can see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Can you -- can I see what you're holding, Usher, please? Could you give me the document the witness has? Yes. That's not right. It's the page before that, please. So you need -- this document consists of a number of pages. No. That's the English. Oh, I see it's copied on the back. Oh, I see. No. Hang on. Okay. Can we have the English on the ELMO, then. Could you read, please, sir, 19 -- the part of the gazette that is 198, and 19 -- you'll need -- usher.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then it carries on.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to read from the beginning?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Yes. I just want you to read the part, to yourself, not aloud, just read it, and then I want to ask you about it. Just read it to yourself.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I think I've got it now. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you read that at the time that it was published in the gazette on the 13th of May, or thereabouts? The gazette came out in June, I think.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally never received copies of the gazette of Republika Srpska in my unit, nor did I see this particular gazette later at any point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You at that time, until certainly General Ninkovic arrived, were in charge of a squadron of planes that was flying combat missions. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was the commander of that squadron.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you telling us that you, as the person in charge of that base, never had drawn to your attention, either by seeing the gazette or by being sent through an order from the Main Staff, this order by Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was not the commander of the whole base. I was only part of that base, located at the Mahovljani airfield. I don't remember having seen this particular Official Gazette at any point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, who was the person who was in charge of the whole base before the arrival of General Ninkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already mentioned the organisation. The officer who was responsible for the logistical support of my unit and for the organisation of the overall work at the airfield was the commander of the base.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And just remind us again of what his name was.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I testified yesterday, Lieutenant Colonel, who later became Colonel, Biga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you saying that any communications from the Main Staff would go -- or from the presidency, would go to this officer rather than you? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Communication between me and Mr. Biga, the commander of the base, concerned only technical aspects of the work, providing adequate conditions for the implementation of my tasks. At the beginning, during the initial stage - and I already stayed that during the months that we are currently discussing, this was the stage when the Yugoslav People's Army was in the process of withdrawal from the territory of the BH. At the same time, the air force was being established and the Army of Republika Srpska was being established and organised. So as for the precise lines of communications and the way that documents were disseminated, it is possible that there were interruptions and problems, because we're talking about a transitional period, a period during which the force was being established. Mr. Biga was not my superior commander. We were collaborators. And the superior command, before the air force and air defence command was established, was the 5th Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you agree that you were the commander of a combat unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you therefore agree that paragraph 2 of this order, "commanders of all units, as well as each member of the army or other armed formation who takes part in combat activities are responsible for the application of the rules of the international law of war"? Do you agree that applied to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that that applied to me as well, but you must also agree with me that it was possible - again, this is my assumption - that someone perhaps assumed that it was not necessary for the air force officers to be apprised of these regulations having to do with prisoners of war. So it was possible that someone deemed it not necessary for me to have such documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where does it say in that paragraph 2 anything about prisoners of war? It is talking, is it not, about the general rules applicable to combat?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. I know that yesterday we discussed the issue of prisoners of war, so I just skimmed this article. I didn't pay attention to details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it is in violation of the rules of international war to bomb hospitals, schools, or anywhere where it is known that non-combatants are present?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully agree with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I want to move on. Yes, thank you. That document can go away. Now, you described to us yesterday - and I'm looking now at the LiveNote at page 19 onwards - the command structure that operated within the air force under -- when it was still part of the JNA. And what you told us was that there was a single line of command, that your immediate superior, as a squadron commander, would have been the regiment commander, the air force regiment; then the corps commander; and then the commander of the air force; and finally, the Main Staff. Do you agree that's an accurate summary?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how it is provided for in the organisation of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. However, you tell us that at the point that we're discussing or talking about, that is, the -- from the formation of the VRS in May of 1992 until you became chief of the air controlling part, that there was in fact no, as it were, intervening level between yourself, as the squadron commander, being directly responsible to the air force command?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the initial period, there was a so-called 5th operational group, which sort of replaced the air force command. It existed for a brief period of time, and later on there was a direct line. So during this period of time, the period of time we are discussing, there was a direct line between the squadron and the air force command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you added that no civilian could give orders to the military, in your case, the air force.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that is clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not including in that, are you, the president of the Republic of Bosnia, as it then was, or of Yugoslavia, or, as it turned out, the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought you were asking me about a civilian from the region of Banja Luka, whether he could, and not that I should explain again the chain of command from the president down to the lowest level. I was -- I thought that you only meant Banja Luka, for that period, and not the system of command in a state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I didn't ask you the questions. In fact, Mr. Cunningham asked you those questions. But I don't want to spend too long on this. The fact is, you didn't mention -- you just said civilians. But you agree, don't you, that the directions to the military, whether the army, the air force, or, if there is a navy, come from civilians through the president of the republic, to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the republic was the supreme commander, and he was a civilian. Everything else, from the supreme commander down to the military staff, is military command. It just happened so that at the time, our president was a civilian, but he could also have been a military man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can I say: I'm not -- I'll make it absolutely clear, I'm not for one moment suggesting to you that a civilian outside the presidency could give a direct order to anybody in the military, but there was, was there not, through the whole chain of command, close cooperation between civilian, political authorities and the military?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period, that was not at my level, so I really wouldn't be able to say what kind of cooperation existed at that, let's say, higher level. It wasn't my level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you can't tell us what cooperation or how matters went on between General Ninkovic and the authorities in Banja Luka, or, for example, General Talic and the authorities in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I couldn't do that. I wasn't informed. I didn't know about that cooperation, and I wasn't present either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You see, I want you just to look at, please, a couple of documents in respect of this. Could you have a look, first of all, please, at P2419.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the best thing is, it's only a part. It's a very large document. It's a part of the report. Usher, if you -- I will -- I've actually marked it for the purposes of the witness, so it's probably easier. And Your Honour, we can put my English copy on the ELMO. That's for the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this is part of a report that was compiled in 1993, on the operation of the various arms of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have, first of all, on the ELMO, the English page 1. And this is the part that deals with the air force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the paragraph I've highlighted for you? "Full coordination was achieved with the commands of the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps, to which we had air force liaison officers and where coordinated action came to the fullest expression, whereas the action in the zones of the other corps was extremely uncertain." And it gives the reasons. Now were you aware of a liaison air force between the air force and the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the former JNA as well, the Yugoslav People's Army, and probably later in the VRS, the establishment did provide for the post of a coordinator, or a representative of the air force in the command unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. Were you aware -- the question is a direct one. Were you pay ware that there was a liaison officer, and my follow-up question is: If you were, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew -- well, not that I knew. There should have been a liaison officer, but I didn't know who he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So nobody told you, as the commander of this squadron, who the liaison officer was with the 1st Krajina Corps? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. As far as I understood, this report is not relevant for the period while I was the squadron commander. This is later, when I was no longer the commander. I said that I didn't see a date anywhere, and you said that this was a report from 2003, as far as I understood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, no. I didn't. This is relevant. It's a report compiled in 1993, on the activities of the VRS since its formation in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. If that is so, then it's relevant. But I really didn't know who the representative of the air force was in the 1st Krajina Corps, and I didn't know his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm sorry, usher. Could you just move the page up for a moment. I just want to see if there's anything else at the end of that. Yes. Now, then, on the next page -- usher, if you can put that up. If I can have the first page back. Thank you. We see some diagrams that show the support. And we look at those -- this is fighter bomber aviation focussed on performing missions in close air-fire support to ground units, as shown in the following charts. And then there's the first chart. There is an explanation given of what the various boxes mean. And this is a survey of the fighter-bomber fire and reconnaissance operations. Do you see that in respect of the 1st Krajina Corps, the fighter-bombers, or the fighter-bombers carried out some 539 operations, which were some kind of combat operation; 24 aerial reconnaissance; and a total -- I see then there's a total all together. In fact, the support by the air force given to the 1st Krajina Corps was the greatest, was it not, of any of the other corps, as you can see from this diagram?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see the diagram. And according to the diagram - and I see it for the first time - but according to that diagram, yes, it does seem that way. I just have to add that the fire support, the operations of all the flights or the aircraft, this is not only combat or fighter-bombers, but helicopters are also included. So I think that this actually -- this number actually includes all types of aircraft, although there is marking there, LBH. I thought that this was perhaps an overall figure, since I'm seeing it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we get to the next page, you'll see that this has got nothing to do with helicopters. These were missions flown by your squadron. Your unit was in fact the largest, wasn't it, air force unit in the whole of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the only fighter-bomber unit; not the biggest, but the only such unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And therefore, whilst you were there, before you went to control of the airport, you and your men flew a very large number of missions, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At this stage, before I was transferred, there were no flights practically being carried out in the BH, in this stage of May to June, because already in June I was already carrying out the transfer of duty, so I practically didn't fly in that period at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were not transferred until August of 1992. Are you telling this Court that from June onwards you never flew a mission, a combat mission?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying that I, as a pilot, did not participate. But what I'm saying is that I did not command those operations. As a pilot, though, I did take part in them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were many missions flown, weren't there, by the air force, during the month particularly of July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there were. I don't know what you mean by the term "a large number of missions," but there were missions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you what I mean shortly. Can we just finish this report? Can we move to the next diagram, if we just push it up slightly. That shows the number and percentage of missions, and as you've already accepted, you were the only fighter squadron in the VRS. It shows a total of -- it's in tonnes of missiles. I'm sorry. I said missions. Missiles, 278 tonnes, 45 per cent of the total expended in support of the cause. And I think the final diagram, if we can have a look at that, please. Yes. Well, it's the number of hours, and I don't think we need bother about that. Now, then can we go, please, to the next part of this report, the next page in English. If I could have that back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if Your Honours have that report with you, it's page 136 onwards that I'm looking at. Page 138.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are following you from the document itself, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour. Put it on the ELMO for the non-existent public. Right. The report then -- I'm sorry, usher. Can you bring it down slightly. No. I mean I want to see the top of the right. Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then we see under the third paragraph: "Coordination and concerted action of bomber-fighter aviation and the command of the 1st KK in preparing and executing all operations were exemplary thanks in part to the existence of air force liaison. I'm going to ask you again so I know you've answered: Are you sure you don't remember there being an air force liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that he existed, but I don't know who he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then, sorry, can we just go to the bottom of the page again, usher, just in case. Yes. And altogether fighter-bomber aviation has carried out 1.205 sorties, in the course of the war, dropped 612.5 tonnes of explosive, meaning that on average, every pilot made 83 sorties, 40 -- it must be put in 40 hours' flying and dropped about 40 tonnes of explosive. That -- and accepting this is taking it up to 1993, does that sound accurate to you, from your own personal experience?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm seeing this data for the first time, so I cannot comment on it. I don't know the exact period. Perhaps you did say it and I didn't hear. I don't know the exact period that this actually refers to, these totals. But if they're here, all this data, then it's probably true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you see underneath that, and that's why I said to you this has nothing to do with helicopters, you will see that there is a separate chart for the sorties down done by helicopters. And over the next page, at 139, there is a chart. Now, before I show you the next part of this document, it's right, isn't it, that at this stage, 1992, 1993, indeed I think for most of the war, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had no air force?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not an air force of this kind, but according to my information, it did have some light sports aircraft which they adapted and made into small fighter planes. The types of planes which we had in the Army of Republika Srpska and which we still have, they didn't have at that time and they don't have them now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You inherited the -- you, the VRS, inherited the power, the fly power, of the JNA; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, yesterday you told us that you and General Ninkovic did not see eye to eye. This is at page 31 of the LiveNote?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't worry about the page, because he said that more than once.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just -- in case Mr. Cunningham wants to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, finally, on this report, could you have a look at subparagraph 8.2, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What page, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Page 141 in the English. It's headed "combat morale." And the English is there. Thank you. It's marked for you. A.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The morale of air force and AA defence unit," anti-aircraft I take it, "was influenced by numerous factors, the most important being a large number of our members were of the opinion that the VRS should have remained unified in all Serbian lands and that no division should have been undertaken in view of all the consequences which later resulted in connections with pressures from the international community." And so that reflects, does it, a view that all the Serbian armies, or armies consisting of Serbs, should have remained united as one army?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less. However, if I may add, the title itself indicated the fact that the VRS was already established. So this was a separate army, the Army of Republika Srpska. The army of Yugoslavia is over there, and then in the Croatian Krajina was the Serbian army of -- I don't know the exact title.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. And now finally, there's one other paragraph which perhaps you could look it, which comes at the very end of this particular paragraph. I've marked that as well. You'll see in orange. If we could have the English up. It's page 142. Just the top, please. And there we see: "So far, 47 flats of the 103 assigned have been given by the municipality of Banja Luka, which has positively affected air force corps morale." That -- that's my -- at the end to remind myself. But that's a reference, isn't it, to the result of your discussions with Mr. Radic and presumably later discussions by other people?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I assume that this was the case, and one can see that the municipality of Banja Luka met our demands and allocated a number of flats, which are no longer occupied by these members. Because in accordance with the relevant law, the apartments have in the meantime been returned to their original owners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you very much. You can put that document away. Or can I have it back? I think it was my copy. Now, I want to ask you, on the lines of cooperation and the like, whether you were aware --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just left my file ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, that in August, on the 18th of August, 1992, there was a meeting at the office of the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, General Talic, at the forward command post? Did you hear the question?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand it, with whom? Who met with General Talic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Were you aware that on the 18th of August, 1992, there was a meeting involving General Talic, General Ninkovic, Mr. Brdjanin, Colonel Vujinovic, or Lieutenant Colonel Vujinovic, Mr. Radic, Mr. Zupljanin, Mr. Erceg, and other people?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know about it at all. I was already busy with the handover of the duty, of my new duty, the chief of air traffic control, so I did not know about it at all. This is the first news.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If General Ninkovic had to be away from the command, who would be left in charge of operational activities?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the commander is absent from the unit, it is usually his deputy, or the chief of staff, who takes over. As far as I can recall, during that period, Colonel Novak had already taken up his duty as the chief of staff, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your experiences within the air force, and when you yourself were in charge, would it surprise you that there was such a high-level meeting involving civilians and military air force and army and police?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can give you a comment on that question. I didn't occupy a high-level position. A squadron commander is a low-level position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that, but for a certain period of time, however limited, you were the man in charge of operations for the only fighter command, as it were, in the whole of the area? So I'm asking you: From that experience, does it surprise you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with this statement: The -- General Ninkovic and the pilots in Banja Luka had been expelled from Croatia. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to a large extent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since Banja Luka had an airport, they, that is, the air force, were housed at the airport, and they became an integral part of the Army of Republika Srpska; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This cannot be contested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There became a branch of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This is what I already explained, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, that the active senior officers were paid by Yugoslavia? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes. That is true as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was page 15507 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, on this topic, and this is really communication, I'd like you to have a look at P2207.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, again, if the usher can find it, but I've marked the relevant part for the witness on my copy of the B/C/S. I'd still like you to find the English so I can hold mine in English, please. And this was on my list. Your Honour, this was on my list, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm surprised it's not available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you put the English, please, at the fourth page, on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, if you can turn in the document to paragraph 6. It's a report -- or it's an order, I should say, to the 1st Krajina Corps, involving the 1st Krajina Corps. And it deals with the actions that were going to be taken in Kotor Varos on the 16th of July. And do you see, under paragraph 6, air support: "Request fire support and air support through the command of the group of brigades or, in case of a breakdown in communications, call directly the 1st Krajina Corps command or the command of the 5th Operative Group"? And the 5th Operative Group was your -- you were part, weren't you, of that group?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the 5th Operative Group of the air force?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Which, before the air force was established, was a command? Yes, the 5th Operative Group issued orders to the squadron. They were in command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want you now to look -- thank you, sir. That's all I want to ask you about on that -- at a video, please, or part of a video.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the Exhibit P1598, and it's a short part. I think Your Honours have seen on a number of occasions. And it starts -- if you have the transcript with you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- At the second page, where you see reporter Cimerman Ajder, his name is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I want you to watch this video and then I'm going to ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We need the sound. All right. Your Honour, we do actually need the sound, but it appears to have disappeared. Can we -- I think we had better stop. Your Honours, I'm sorry. Could I ask Your Honours to take a short -- the break now while I try and sort this out? May I just say for the record that Sanction is an absolutely appalling tool.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Chuqing is saying that the sound is on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I was told by the technician. Would you like to try again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's try it again, and if it's the case, we continue now; if it's not, unless you prefer to have the break now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm quite happy to go on. I can't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not seeing anything either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is on the video, but there is no sound.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not even on my video thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have the break, because --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I think, Your Honour, we better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There isn't any sound, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner. I suppose you plan to finish with this witness today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll try, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the technical hitch is sorted. Your Honour, when we play it, I wonder if the interpreters could -- normally I say don't interrupt, but on this occasion, I think it would help the part we're going to play. And it's page 2 of Your Honour's transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Of this last night's list of fatalities included Colonel Milan Stevilovic, head of the Department for Intelligence and Security Affairs of the 1st Krajina Corps, Stevan Markovic, head of the police department in the Banja Luka public security station, and Obrad Bubic, a craftsman from Kotor Varos, while Novo Petrusic, a driver, was captured and taken away. In addition, yesterday, in the afternoon hours Djuro Eskic, an employee of Proleter --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. The witness needs to hear the B/C/S. At the moment, I don't know whether he is hearing B/C/S. Can I just ask?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was interpretation, but there was no image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, it's getting complicated, Ms. Korner. Usher, please. Let's start again, and make sure that he is receiving whatever is shown in video mode in his own language. I was receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Of the 1st Krajina Corps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you hear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to go a little bit further, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Just last week in this area, mostly in the villages of Vecici, Vranici, Sokoline, and Rujevica, 17 soldiers and members of the special police unit were killed. Last night's list of fatalities included Colonel Milan Stevilovic, head of the Department for Intelligence and Security Affairs of the 1st Krajina Corps, Stevan Markovic, head of the police department in the Banja Luka public security station, and Obrad Bubic, a craftsman from Kotor Varos, while Novo Petrusic, a driver, was captured and taken away. In addition, yesterday, in the afternoon hours, Djuro Eskic an employee of Proleter, was killed in Kotor Varos by a sniper shooting from Kotor on the left bank of the Vrbanja River. Last year during the clearing of the terrain in villages inhabited by Muslims and Croats in Kotor Varos municipality the fiercest battles were waged in the very same village of Vecici. Yesterday and today aviation of Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina took part in the final operations conducted jointly by the troops of the Serbian Republic of BH and special police units firing at select enemy targets. The number of fatalities among the Muslim Croat paramilitary has exceeded 300, with a significantly greater number of wounded. In yesterday's and today's combat alone Muslim and Croat extremists had over 100 wounded and killed and about 200 wounded. Their own civilians, Muslim women, children, and the elderly are held hostage by the extremists who tortured and killed them. Yesterday, between 1.600 and 1.000 -- between 1600 and 1700 hours in the vicinity of Rujevica village on the road between Maslovare and Kotor Varos extreme cruelty enemy villains ambushed and tormented to death Stevan Markovic and Obrad Bubic, also killing Milan Stevilovic and capturing Nova Petrusic. A commemoration ceremony was held today in honour of Milan Stevilovic at the Banja Luka JNA Hall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, that's all I want to show you. Can I explain to you, as you're probably no doubt aware, this was filmed in July of 1992, around the time that Lieutenant Colonel Stevilovic was killed. Do you remember that period?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that he was killed. I think that he was either a colonel or a lieutenant colonel. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Those planes we saw dropping bombs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I saw the witness hinting at something. Was there anything wrong? Is something wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have anything on my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to -- I understood that he needs to go back. All right. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, those planes we saw carrying out that attack in Kotor Varos were your squadron, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were part of the air force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, yesterday when you were asked whether you took part in the attack on Kotor Varos, before you said no, there was a hesitation. I'm going to ask you again, and if you don't want to reply to that question, you can seek Their Honours' leave. Were you one of the pilots who took part in that attack?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you send your pilots to take part in that attack?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I was not in the unit, when those few days -- so during those days, this attack, or this sortie or sorties, probably took place over those few days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, where were you at the beginning of July 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to say precisely, but I was in the middle of transferring my duties in the work of the command. So I was in the broader area of Banja Luka. I wasn't at the airport all the time. I also used to go to the air force command. I was going to the premises where the air force command was being formed, so I was working on some documents. So I wasn't in any fixed place. I cannot remember exactly where I was on that date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. Are you saying it took well over a month for you to transfer from your operational duties as squadron leader to taking over the flight control at the airport?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't take that long, but it was done parallel. All of these things were being done at the same time, the stage when the air force was being formed, the transfer of my duties as commander, and then accepting other duties as chief of the flight control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm hearing something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Don't worry. For some reason, these machines today have a life of their own. Sir, you were aware, weren't you, that in the course of these attacks, civilians - men, women, and children - were killed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to show you now one other -- I'm sorry. Just before we move on: What kind of missiles were being dropped that we saw in that video? What kind of bombs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this footage, if I can see that precisely, this is the Orao aircraft, so it would be dropping napalm bombs, fire bombs, as far as I know. So I think that it is these bombs that are being used here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked whether you dropped any bombs that had I think a chemical component yesterday, or words to that effect. I can find it, if necessary. And you said no. What do you call napalm?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The question had to be with chemical munitions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Chemical munitions. What do you call napalm, please, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chemical munitions is something that I understand to mean - and that's how it was with us - as bombs which contain combat poisons, chemical poisons. A napalm bomb is something that did not contain toxic materials, poisons. A bomb contains fuel, liquid fuel, and a fuse that sets this charge off, and it goes off. So as far as I know, napalm doesn't contain any toxins which take a long time to act. A napalm bomb is an incendiary, short-action means which just burns out and doesn't leave any lasting effects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but has an effect, doesn't it, on the persons who might be in the path of or affected by the explosion of that bomb?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bomb doesn't explode. There is no classic explosion, but there is an incendiary, there is an instantaneous flame, and this is a classic flame, a fire, which then burns out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see photographs of what happened in the Vietnam war?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The effects of napalm on people?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure now whether that's the same type of napalm on the same size of the bomb, and so on. I did see people with burns, but I cannot say exactly what type of bomb was used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want you to look now, please, at a short clip from a second video. The number of that is 2431.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours should have a transcript. It's a very short passage on the first page of the transcript. And again, if the interpreters could just interpret what is said when we get to it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] An entire family is in the grave, an entire family, father, child, and wife. They were killed by a shell.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause it there, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] In the first attack by aircraft --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, what's that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is a cluster bomb, although the image is not very sharp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll play it, the rest of it, and I think you'll see it is. [Videotape played]. One of those cluster bombs, here's is one of these cluster bombs. It contains somewhere around 200 of these explosives. There you have it. This is what they, the Chetniks, sent, humanitarian aid. You will see up there, there is napalm too. That's worse than ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, that was a cluster bomb. Tell the Court, please, what a cluster bomb is.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A cluster bomb is a classic bomb which contains -- a bomb which contains classic explosives, and consists of a number of smaller bombs, bomblets. So it's a kind of cluster containing several bomblets. I cannot recall the exact weight of it, but it could be ranging from 100 to 150 kilogrammes. And the Orao model aircraft would carry a cluster bomb. That's the one that I saw on film, and I just wanted to inform you that I did not fly that type of aircraft. A cluster bomb, I repeat again, is a classic bomb. It does not contain any other chemical agents, other than -- besides classic explosives. So it's a bomb containing exclusively classic explosives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Designed to cause maximum injury and damage; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All bombs are designed to cause as much injury as possible, and destruction, and so one of those types of bombs is a cluster bomb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to drop such a bomb on a hospital would clearly be a war crime, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely agree that it would be a war crime to drop such a bomb on a hospital. I am a father and a grandfather, and for me, that is inconceivable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to show it, but if Your Honours look at page 14 of the video -- of the transcript, you'll see there's a reference to it. All right. Thank you. Now I want to move, please, to a later or different events, the SOS, their arrival in Banja Luka. You told the Court yesterday, as you did in the interview, that your contact with the SOS, or your first awareness of the SOS, was that there was a checkpoint near the airport and you were stopped. And what you said to us at page 36 was this: "They introduced themselves." How did they introduce themselves?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They simply said: Sir, these are units which are checking the approaches to town. They're manning the checkpoints. And please just tell us where you intend to go. I responded that I was an officer, a major, and that I was going to the airport. And they said: Well, no. There are no problems. Please go ahead. You can pass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say they said they were units. What, they told you that they were units of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it wasn't interpreted correctly. They just said: We are a unit monitoring the exits and entrances to town. They said: Where are you going? I said I was an officer, I was going to the airport. And they said: No. There are no problems. And I thought that the fact that they were just monitoring or manning the checkpoint, I didn't think that there was anything significant about that. I didn't attach too much importance to it. I saw checkpoints later, throughout the war, there was a checkpoint in the area of Zaluzani also, and at another place I cannot recall exactly where.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the first checkpoint that you had seen preventing access to the airport?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the first checkpoint located exactly where the road from Banja Luka towards the airport ends, the four-lane road, and then it turns into a dual-lane road. It becomes a more narrow road, and that's where the checkpoint was located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that you believed that these men were regular JNA units?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since they were wearing camouflage uniforms, just like the members of any army or unit throughout the former Yugoslavia and anywhere in the world would wear, I assumed that it was just another land forces unit. I didn't attach any significance to this. I didn't have any problems at that checkpoint on the road, and then ask later why these problems happened. I simply passed through. As far as I can remember, there were a few cars parked on the side with the trunk of the cars open, but I didn't have any problems. I was driving in a Zastava 101 vehicle, and I just passed through. I didn't attach any importance to that. It wasn't anything I thought that was important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, but they weren't wearing regular uniform, camouflage uniform, were they? To this extent, you were asked yesterday what sort of headgear they were wearing, and you said that they were wearing caps, or a kind of smaller type of headgear. They were wearing red berets, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember them wearing red berets. They wore a kind of small hat or cap which you could also -- you could put the flaps down over your ears, something like that. I don't recall it being a red beret.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember being asked about this in your interview of July 2001?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you can see it, if necessary. It's page 19, Your Honours. You were asked: "Do you recall seeing red berets in front of the municipal building, or generally in Banja Luka at that time?" "Yes, you replied, not in front of the municipal building, but yes, I saw the men with red berets, and in camouflage uniforms, and I thought it was some unit of the 1st Krajina Corps. I took it for granted. Probably I was also in a uniform, in a car with military plates and insignia. They never stopped me or had any contact. I never had any contacts with them." Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then you were telling us they were wearing red berets. Today and yesterday you tell us they weren't wearing red berets. Which is correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that they had red berets at that checkpoint. That's what it should have stated here. I did used to see people in camouflage uniforms and with red berets around in the town. So this was not specifically about that checkpoint. I didn't see people with red berets perhaps in front of the municipal building, but I did see them going down the streets throughout the town, and I saw them around, and I believed that they belonged to some unit of the Krajina Corps. I wasn't thinking of anything else. I thought it was a unit -- not a unit, but I thought that they belonged to the ground forces and they had the uniforms. At that point, there were different types of caps and hats, and caps were something that was worn the least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you know the politician Milorad Dodik?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know who he is now, I take it.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at the time, you weren't aware that he was carrying out guard duties at the airport as part of his conscription; is that right? You didn't know that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't know. But then later, after the war, at some assembly, he stated that at the assembly that he was also a member of the army and that he was at the airport. I never met him personally. I don't know him personally to this day. I know of him as a politician.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see his testimony at this Court at all?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only when I was watching the evening -- the news broadcast I saw some excerpts, but I did not listen to the entire testimony. I just heard a news item stating that he did testify. I apologise, but if I can explain. During the day, I am mostly taking care of my grandchild. I go out for walks and things. So during the day I'm not really at home much. I am at home in the evenings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The SOS didn't just set up a barricade, did they? They turned up at the airport itself.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise again, but I'm saying that at that first, initial period, I didn't know that this was the SOS, the Serbian defence forces. They probably had contacts with the commander of the airport, and that Mr. Dodik was probably part of that service at the airport, and they probably cooperated with them. The rear unit and the logistics unit was in charge of providing security for my personnel and my equipment. I didn't have any special unit or staff who guarded me and my men. This was done by the logistics unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Sir, that day, when the SOS arrived and you were stopped at the barricade, you were at the airport, weren't you, on the 3rd of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just told us you were because you were stopped by them on the way to the airport.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was going there. Yes, I said I was at the airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you telling us, sir, that you were wholly unaware, whilst you were at the airport, that this group of men had taken over control of the airport?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A group of people taking control of the airport, in spite of all of the units that were there at the airport. I'm hearing of this for the first time. Besides the police, the military police, the defence forces to guard the airport, and members of the logistics base, this is something that I'm hearing of for the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm suggesting to you, sir, that that -- this is not the first time that you've heard it but that they were allowed by you, the military police, and everybody else at the airport, to take control.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in no position to permit something like that. I said that before. It's possible that the military police cooperated with them, but I wasn't authorised to permit them to do that, and I had no idea that they had taken over. Nobody came to me and said: We have taken over the airport. Nobody came to me and said anything like that. And I don't know what exactly this term "taking over the airport" refers to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will put it to you in the clearest possible terms, sir, that they were allowed to control the flights, what took off, who was allowed to take off, and the whole airport was ruled for that period of time 24 hours or perhaps a little longer by them. That's what I'm suggesting. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that they were controlling the take-offs and landings of civilian aircraft, but not of military aircraft. Perhaps they controlled the civilian flights at that time. Perhaps that was so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to the airport, did you make any inquiries of anybody as to who these men were and why there was a barricade at the airport?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Weren't you interested as to why the airport was being barricaded off?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't think that the airport was being barricaded off. The airport is not six kilometres away from Banja Luka. The airport was about 20 kilometres away from Banja Luka. The barricades ended some six to ten kilometres away. I did not believe that the airport was being blocked off by this barricade. The barricade was closer to Banja Luka than the airport. After the barricade, there was a bridge to the right, leading to Prnjavor and Derventa. I didn't believe that the barricade -- and since I didn't have any problems, I didn't attach any significance to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You told us --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I just wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I apologise for the interruption. I didn't want it to get too far away. Page 40, line 17, there was an addition to his answer that was not translated. He added at the end of the statement: Perhaps that was so. The following: But I did not have any control over civilian flights. And I would like to see if the witness can confirm that. And again, I apologise for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, did you hear -- did you follow what Mr. Cunningham said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And have you indeed stated this, in addition to what we have on the -- in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed, Ms. Korner. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday, sir, that a while went by before you found out that these men were not affiliated to or not members of any of the 1st Krajina Corps units. When did you find that out? What do you mean by "a while"?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A while. I can say that it was approximately six months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. So are you telling us that you were wholly unaware, between April and September 1992, of the SOS presence in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether I knew about the presence of the SOS, I kept thinking that it was one of the units, since they wore camouflage uniforms and everything. I believe that it was one of the units of the 1st Krajina Corps. Not a unit, but I felt that these were people who belonged to the 1st Krajina Corps. I never saw them together in a larger group. I didn't see any of the units in a larger group together, say 50 or 100 men lined up at one time. I didn't have the possibility of seeing something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were completely unaware of the demands that they submitted to the authorities of Banja Luka on the 3rd of April; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know. You mean the municipal, civilian authorities of Banja Luka. No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were completely unaware of the fact that one of their demands, the appointment of a crisis staff, was acceded to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know. If you said the date as the 3rd or the 4th of April, no, I didn't know it at the time. I didn't know that there was such requests on the 3rd of April. I didn't know that it had been made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nenad Stevandic, you tell us, was one of the acquaintances that you had made shortly after arriving in Banja Luka in 1991. He was friends of friends, you told us.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were unaware that he was appointed to this early crisis staff at the beginning of April?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You -- do I take it from that that you never listened to the radio, never watched Banja Luka news, and never read a newspaper during the -- this particular period, at the beginning of April?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can't say that I never did that. I don't know whether I happened to do so then, when it was broadcast on television. I don't know whether I watched television then. I told you yesterday that due to technical problems and the position of the airport in relation to the repeater, watched Croatian television more. We had better reception. But to tell you the truth, we didn't really feel up to watching television and reading newspapers that much. We were dealing with much more responsible things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you read a newspaper, I take it it was Glas newspaper you read.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Actually, I think -- well, I did read Glas, but I think that we read Vecernje Novosti, a Belgrade-based paper. I don't know how. It must have been the logistics unit that managed to obtain this paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in 1992, you were age, I think, 38. Is that right? Sir? You were born in 1944, I think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In 1954.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 1954. Hang on, Your Honour. I'll find the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1955. Correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, he was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: According to the Defence, he was born on 22nd of October, 1946.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know how you managed that, sir. Weren't you born as you told us on the 5th of December, 1955?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the correct date, the 5th of December, 1955, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the Defence you were born in October -- what was the date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the summary distributed by Mr. Cunningham shows him as being born on the 22nd of October of 1946.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, it's remarkable, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I don't know where I got that date. I thought I got it off the witness sheet that we had provided to the Court. It was obviously a misstatement on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay, but the witness has confirmed that he was born in 1955 anyways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992 you were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He was 48.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 38, Your Honour. I think I'm right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 38, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I thought I was right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nenad Stevandic was a much younger man, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 37. I apologise. I apologise, but I was 37 in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nenad Stevandic was a much, much younger man, wasn't he, in his very early 20s?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how old he is. I don't know when he was born. I didn't know him enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He's a medical student, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean, I can only assume that at the time he was a student, because now he's a physician. He works at the medical centre in Banja Luka as a physician.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you and he became friendly, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period do you have in mind when you say we became friendly? Because I was never really friends with Nenad Stevandic. We were acquaintances or colleagues. It's difficult to say that we were really friends. He was a very good friend of a friend of mine. We were never really close, nor do we see each other now, nor did we continue to see each other after the war. We may have seen each other in passing, but we are not in permanent contact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were aware that he headed, weren't you, something called the Sokol Society?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that a sports association called Sokol Society was established in Banja Luka at one point, that it was an old, traditional sports association, Serbian sports association, dedicated to promoting sports spirit, and culture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was in fact, wasn't it, to your knowledge, sir, I suggest, the youth wing of the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know it was the youth wing of the SDS. The Sokol Society is an ancient society, dedicated to the sports and sports spirit amongst the Serbian people. I was never a member of the Sokol Society. I never had any contact with the Sokol Society and I didn't live in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You told us you did live in Banja Luka, you had a flat in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the previous 20 years. That's what I had in mind. I was not a member of such a society, and there was no Sokol Society in Mostar. That's what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw the SOS in Banja Luka, the men with red berets, did you appreciate that these men were thugs and criminals?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Excuse me. I never thought that any of those individuals who wore red berets was a criminal. I just thought that they were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'd like you to have a look, please, at part of a report, Exhibit P400, please. And I'll give you the marked -- if you look at page 5 of that report in B/C/S, and if we could have the English version on the ELMO. It's the 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, the 8th page. And if you, sir, can look in your copy at page 5. It's the third paragraph, beginning "the SOS." If you can just read it to yourself, please, and let me know when you've finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Usher. Usher, can you move it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You've got the -- yes, that's the part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is a report that was done by the chief of intelligence of the VRS. Were you aware that Nenad Stevandic had, let's put it this way, connections with this group of men called the SOS?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you never discussed with him his activities in respect of either political, or any others?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the period that you are discussing, I didn't discuss political activities with anyone. When I had time, I only had informal, private conversations with my friends and acquaintances. I never discussed politics, nor did I believe it to be appropriate to discuss politics with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were completely unaware, as with everything else about the SOS, of any connection between Stevandic; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You can put -- give that document back to the usher. Thank you. Now, Dubocanin, the gentleman who came to ask you, with a friend, to join the Crisis Staff. You told us he was somebody else that you had met when you first came to Banja Luka at the end of 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was at the end of 1991, but in early 1992. I couldn't tell you the precise date. Because it was a long time ago, I really cannot tell you precisely when it was that I met -- that I first met with someone. It's really difficult for me to recall at this point. A lot of things happened between 1990 and today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described him as the late Dubocanin, Slobodan Dubocanin. When did he die?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it is a bit awkward for me, but I simply cannot recall when it was that he died. I only know that he died a natural death, but I really cannot recall the year in which he died, and it would not be appropriate for me to give you the wrong date. I mean --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Don't worry about that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to be respectful about the dead. Lots of my friends, including lots of pilots, died, and I'm getting mixed up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What did Mr. Dubocanin do when you first met him? What was his job?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first met him -- I mean, when I first met him, I could tell by his insignia that he had the rank of captain. I thought he was the commander of a unit there. I never asked him precisely what he was. I just thought that he was the commander of a KOV unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can you just explain, before I move on: What's a KOV unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It refers to land forces. KOV means land forces, a land forces unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You thought he was part of the JNA, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you realise that he too was connected with the SOS?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nothing for me to realise. I didn't know at the time of this SOS. I just knew that he was an officer, a captain, belonging to the land forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't you ask him what he was a captain in?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never asked him a specific question, but I think I remember him saying that he was a commander of a unit located in Kotor Varos, to the best of my recollection. A land forces unit, an infantry unit, located in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He became part, didn't he, of the squad known as the Special Intervention Unit of the CSB?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
